hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Butter and cheese can provide the same amount of saturated fat and have different effects on LDL cholesterol. Why?

That question gets at something I think we’re missing in many of our debates about nutrition: the food itself.

I sat down with Dr. Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist, nutrition scientist, and director of the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University. This is one of the most important nutrition podcasts I’ve ever recorded.

We spend so much time talking about carbs, fat, and protein. But foods also contain vitamins, minerals, fiber, polyphenols, and many other compounds whose effects we’re only beginning to understand. How those components are packaged together and what processing does to that structure can change how a food affects our bodies.

This is the “food matrix.” It helps explain why judging a food by its saturated fat content alone can be misleading, and why adding protein to an ultra-processed snack doesn’t automatically make it healthy.

One of the things I found most fascinating was how processing can change what we absorb and what reaches our gut bacteria.

We also get into seed oils, red and processed meat, what may be driving obesity, and a question that matters whenever we evaluate a dietary fat: what are we eating in its place?

I learned a lot from this conversation, including things that changed how I think about some foods that contain saturated fat. I’m excited for you to hear it.

Links to the episode on all platforms are in the comments below.

One of the simplest ways to support your sleep starts in the morning - get outside into bright light for 10-15 minutes, minimum.

Light reaching your eyes helps synchronize the master clock in your brain. That clock helps coordinate daily rhythms throughout your body, including hormone release, metabolism, and the timing of sleep.

Cortisol is part of that rhythm. It gets a bad reputation because we associate it with stress, but its normal morning rise helps prepare you to wake up and become active.

Your body also needs a clear signal for when the day ends, so melatonin can rise and help prepare you for sleep.

Give that system a consistent schedule by waking up around the same time each day, getting outdoor light soon after waking when daylight is available, and keeping lights dimmer as bedtime approaches.

hits.name: Benjamin Bikman
hits.text:
Most men are told that an enlarging prostate is just what happens with age and male hormones.

That leaves something unexplained. Every man ages and every man has those hormones, yet some end up with a much larger gland than others.

In human studies, insulin keeps showing up.

In a Swedish clinic study of 307 men with urinary symptoms, prostate growth was faster in those with type 2 diabetes, obesity, and low HDL. When the men were grouped by fasting insulin, growth rose with each step up. After the other factors were weighed together, only age and fasting insulin stood out as independent predictors of prostate size.

A study in men without diabetes found a similar pattern. Higher fasting insulin went with a larger prostate, even when blood sugar looked normal.

Insulin resistance alone is enough to expose the prostate to high insulin, and that state is common in middle-aged men. Insulin is a growth signal. When it stays high for years, prostate cells keep getting that message to build and divide.

Metabolic syndrome tracks with this too. In a meta-analysis of more than 5,000 men, those with metabolic syndrome had larger prostates, with the biggest difference in the inner zone that wraps around the urethra.

This is observational human data. It does not prove that lowering insulin shrinks every prostate. Even so, it's a good reason to watch fasting insulin and waist size well before night-time bathroom trips become routine.
hits.draft_en:
Ben Bikman makes a point every bloke over 50 should hear: a growing prostate isn't just "age and hormones".

In a Swedish study of 307 men, only two things stood out as independent predictors of prostate size: age and fasting insulin. Higher insulin, bigger gland, even when blood sugar looked normal.

He's honest that it's observational and doesn't prove lowering insulin shrinks every prostate. But you can't change your age. You can change your waist.

Next blood test, ask for fasting insulin, not just sugar. Better to know before the 3am dunny trips start.

I was a great meat-eater. For years I believed I could not live without it. My health was poor—I fainted easily, felt weak and dizzy between meals—and a piece of flesh seemed the only thing that restored my strength. I thought it indispensable.

Then, on June 6, 1863, the Lord gave me a comprehensive vision on health reform. He showed me that the diet of flesh foods was not His original plan for man, that it was injurious to body and soul, and that His commandment-keeping people were to receive a reform diet. 

Disease and suffering would be lessened as they accepted it. The light was clear: eating the flesh of dead animals animalizes the system, strengthens the lower passions, beclouds the intellect, and corrupts the blood. Animals themselves were increasingly diseased—filled with tuberculosis, cancer, and parasites—and those who ate them took those diseases into their own bodies. Cancers, tumors, and inflammatory diseases were largely the result of this gross living.

I acted at once. Meat was cut from my table. I wrote and spoke the counsel: “Flesh meat is not necessary for health or strength.” The simple grains, fruits, and vegetables contain all the nutritive properties needed to make good blood. God permitted animal food after the Flood in part to shorten the lives of a corrupt race, but it was never the best food. In a land of abundance, there is no need to live on corpses.

I was careful. I never made it a test of fellowship. I said plainly that I would not declare no one should ever taste meat under any circumstances, for that would be carrying matters to extremes. Yet the principle stood: God’s people were to take a firm stand against meat-eating for their spiritual and physical good. 

Our sanitariums and medical institutions were to educate on this question. The Battle Creek Sanitarium, later Loma Linda, and the whole health work grew from that light. Physicians and workers trained there carried the message outward.

That counsel shaped the Seventh-day Adventist health system. The Adventist Health Studies that followed—large, long-term observations of our people—have been widely cited in discussions of plant-based diets, longevity, and chronic disease. Loma Linda itself became known as one of the “Blue Zones.” 

What began as a vision in 1863 entered the broader conversation about nutrition, fiber, and the supposed superiority of a non-flesh diet. The light given then still stands in our institutions and in the research they produced.

Lakshmi’s hands tell the rest of the story.
In the morning I walk to the shed near Kollam. The floor is already covered with roasted nuts. I squat the way my mother taught me, knees bent, back rounded, and begin. One shell, then the next. The wooden tool or the cutter cracks them open. That is when the oil comes.

The skin thickens and cracks. My nails pit. I rub ash on my hands before I start, the way everyone does. It helps a little. Gloves would slow me down, and we are paid by the kilo, not by the hour. If I shell or peel only six or seven kilos, the money is not enough. On a good day I manage ten or twelve. Many days the factory has fewer nuts and we are sent home early.

By afternoon my back is locked and my knees throb. The pain in my wrists and fingers does not stop when I stand up. At home I wash my hands again and again, but the stain stays. The burning can continue into the night. I cook rice, look after my mother, and try to sleep on my side so my back does not seize.

Deep in the rainforest along the Andirá and Marau rivers (Amazonas and Pará states), boys around 12 years old undergo this coming-of-age ordeal to become men, warriors, hunters, and eligible for marriage and leadership. The Sateré-Mawé (roughly 13,000–17,000 people) are also famous as the people who first cultivated guaraná. 
The Ant and the Pain
The ritual centers on the bullet ant (Paraponera clavata), a large black ant whose sting ranks at the extreme top of the Schmidt sting pain index. Entomologist Justin Schmidt famously described a single sting as “pure, intense, brilliant pain… like walking over flaming charcoal with a three-inch nail embedded in your heel.” The pain can last 12–24 hours (hence the local name “24-hour ant”), often with swelling, temporary paralysis, nausea, trembling, or hallucinations. The venom’s key peptide, poneratoxin, keeps pain receptors firing long after most other insect stings fade. 
Preparing the Gloves
Men collect the ants from the forest, often smoking them out of their colonies. The ants are then submerged in a plant mixture (commonly involving cashew leaves) that sedates them for a short time. While quiet, dozens of them—sometimes around 80 or more—are carefully woven into gloves made of plant fibers or palm fronds, stingers pointing inward. The gloves are often decorated with macaw or hawk feathers. Once the ants wake, they are furious and ready to sting. 
The Ordeal
The boy slips his hands into the gloves and must keep them on for about 10 minutes (sometimes described as longer). During this time the community sings and dances with him around a pole or in a circle to help him endure. Showing pain or weakness is discouraged if he hopes to be seen as strong enough for leadership. Afterward his hands and arms may be swollen and temporarily paralyzed. The effects can linger for a day or more. 
This is not a one-time test. To complete the initiation he must repeat the ritual roughly 20 times, spread over months or even years. Only then is he considered a full man in the eyes of the community. 
Meaning
In Sateré-Mawé belief the ordeal builds physical and mental strength, proves courage, and functions almost like a spiritual “vaccine” that protects against illness and makes a better hunter and protector of the people and forest. A man who has not undergone it is sometimes viewed as unlucky or incomplete. Women participate in supporting roles (gathering materials, preparing drinks such as guaraná-based çapó), but the glove itself is for the boys. 
The ritual has been documented by anthropologists, National Geographic, and others (including adventurer Steve Backshall), and it continues today as a living tradition tied to cultural identity and the defense of ancestral lands.

It is an extreme, voluntary test of endurance rooted in a specific Amazonian culture—not a universal Indigenous practice. The pain is real and severe, but participants view it as transformative.

In the forests of the Brazilian and Venezuelan Amazon, the Yanomami still hunt and eat monkeys even when fruit trees are heavy with food.
The canopy around their villages is full of palms, figs, and other fruiting trees. People gather and eat those fruits, and they grow plantains and manioc in gardens. Yet meat—especially monkey meat—remains highly valued. Spider monkeys (Ateles belzebuth) are among the preferred game. Hunters say the meat tastes good, particularly when the animals are fat after feeding on seasonal fruits. Howler monkeys, peccaries, and birds are also taken. Large monkeys are relatively easy to locate because they travel in noisy groups, and their size makes the effort worthwhile. 
Men leave the village with bows, arrows, or (increasingly) guns. When they return with spider monkeys, the animals are often tied into a seated position, smoked or roasted, and shared. On big feasts tied to the peach-palm harvest, hunters have returned with dozens of spider monkeys alongside other game. Monkeys also appear in Yanomami mythology, technology, and adornment; some groups were historically called “monkey eaters” by outsiders because the practice was so characteristic. 
The same pattern appears among other Amazonian peoples. The Waorani (Huaorani) of Ecuador hunt large-bodied primates with blowguns and share the meat widely between households. The Shipibo of Peru list woolly and spider monkeys among preferred foods. Across the region, groups deliberately hunt monkeys when fruit is abundant precisely because that is when the animals are fattest. Plant foods and fish form the bulk of many diets by weight, but meat carries special cultural weight—status, sharing obligations, and a distinct sense of satisfaction that fruit alone does not provide.
This is not a matter of scarcity. The forests are productive in fruit, yet the preference for animal protein, fat, and the social value of hunting persists. Different groups maintain different taboos (some avoid tapir or deer while favoring monkey; neighbors reverse the pattern), using food choices partly as a way to mark identity. The result is that monkeys continue to be hunted and eaten in places surrounded by fruit.

The practice continues today in many remote communities, though firearms and population pressure have reduced some primate populations. Meat from monkeys and other game remains a central part of subsistence and culture for these groups.

Did you know your fat tissue can hold on to signs of past obesity, even after major weight loss?

In people who lost weight after bariatric surgery, fat cells continued to show some of the changes in gene activity associated with their previous obesity.

A similar pattern appeared in mice. The mouse experiments also found persistent changes in the chemical marks that help regulate gene activity. After losing weight, previously obese mice regained it faster when exposed to a high-fat diet again.

The distinction between the human and mouse findings matters. Persistent changes in gene activity were demonstrated in human fat tissue. The detailed evidence for an epigenetic memory, and the experiments connecting prior obesity with faster weight regain, came from mice.

Insulin is central to all of this. It is the main hormone telling fat cells to store fat and to hold on to the fat they already have. When insulin is high, fat cells take in more fat and release less of it. Even a modest rise in insulin can sharply slow the release of stored fat.

That matters most after weight loss. A fat cell that has been through obesity may be primed to refill quickly. If insulin stays high from frequent eating or a diet built on refined carbohydrates, those cells get the signal they need to regain what they lost.

Keeping insulin low has the opposite effect. Fat cells can keep releasing stored fat, and hunger tends to be easier to manage.

This study does not tell us how long those changes persist in people or which habits might reverse them. It does give another reason to treat weight maintenance as its own phase, with insulin control at the center of it.

outsiders.text:
Introducing GR00T 2: our most advanced, open System One model for robotics. It runs entirely on your robot’s onboard compute, fully untethered, and you own every weight of it. GR00T 2 features: 

1. Long-horizon tasks: dexterous manipulation and whole-body control chained over 20+ steps and 5+ minutes, such as performing chemistry lab experiments or assembling model airplanes end to end.
2. X-Adapt: adapting from easy data sources (human wearables and simulation) and deploying zero-shot to diverse real robots.
3. Unified Cognition: native integrations with frontier agents for advanced physical reasoning, robust error recovery, and safety monitoring.

It's an open-source buffet! We are releasing not only the model weights and X-Adapt recipes (coming December), but also our agentic framework, simulation engine, annotation engine, hardware design, and even training data (100K hours, that's ~11 yrs of experience), all available today! 

Everything that moves will be autonomous. Anyone can become a roboticist. 

Lock in, build with us!

outsiders.name: Ethan Mollick
outsiders.text:
A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US).

In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened.

The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"
